covers_texts: Yes. A “telephonic sales call” includes a text message (§501.059(1)(j)).
quiet_hours_notes: 8 a.m.–8 p.m. and no more than 3 calls in 24 hours on the same subject (§501.616(6)). That section covers “commercial telephone sellers” and says “phone calls”; it doesn’t mention texts.
consent_limits_optout: Prior express written consent for unsolicited telephonic sales calls that use an automated system to select and dial numbers (§501.059(8)(a)). Before suing over texts, the recipient must reply STOP, and the sender has 15 days to stop (§501.059(10)(c)). $500 per violation or actual damages, up to triple if willful (§501.059(10)).
reply_or_inquiry_carveout: A call isn’t “unsolicited” if it’s made in response to the express request of the person called, or to someone with a prior or existing business relationship (§501.059(1)(k)).

covers_texts: Yes. The consent rules cover solicitations “by telephone call, text message, or voicemail” (§14-4501(d)).
quiet_hours_notes: No solicitations between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., and no more than 3 in 24 hours on the same subject (§14-4502(c)).
consent_limits_optout: Prior express written consent for solicitations that use an automated system to select or dial numbers, or a recorded message (§14-4502(a)(3)). $500 or actual damages, up to triple if willful or knowing (§14-4503).
reply_or_inquiry_carveout: The consent rule doesn’t apply to “a single telephone solicitation made to a customer or client in response to an inquiry or request” (§14-4502(a)(1)(v)). The quiet-hours rule has no such carve-out.

covers_texts: Yes. Oklahoma’s solicitation definitions name cellular text messages (§775A.2), and the Telephone Solicitation Act of 2022 has its own consent rule (§775C.3).
quiet_hours_notes: 8 a.m.–8 p.m. and no more than 3 calls in 24 hours on the same subject (§775C.4). The section says “phone calls.”
consent_limits_optout: Prior express written consent for commercial telephonic sales calls that use an automated dialing system or a recorded message (§775C.3).
reply_or_inquiry_carveout: Not verified by us. Read the definitions in §775C.2 before relying on an exception.

covers_texts: Yes. A “telephone solicitation” includes a text message (ORS 646.561, amended by HB 3865 in 2025).
quiet_hours_notes: 8 a.m.–8 p.m., and no more than 3 solicitations in 24 hours unless you have an established business relationship, meaning a transaction in the last 18 months (ORS 646.563).
consent_limits_optout: You may rely on a mobile number’s area code to decide whether the person is in Oregon (ORS 646.563(2)).
reply_or_inquiry_carveout: Not a telephone solicitation: “a call or text message that responds directly to a message received from a party” (ORS 646.561(4)(b)(D)). The law doesn’t say whether a missed call counts as a “message.”

covers_texts: Yes, from mid-October 2026. Act 47 of 2026 (SB 992), enacted July 20, 2026 and effective 90 days later (around October 18–19), adds text messages, voicemail and ringless voicemail to “telephone solicitation.”
quiet_hours: 9 a.m.–7 p.m.; none on Sundays or holidays (from mid-Oct. 2026)
quiet_hours_notes: No solicitations on Sundays or legal holidays, or before 9 a.m. or after 7 p.m. (SB 992 as passed).
consent_limits_optout: Recipients can opt out by replying STOP, QUIT, END, REVOKE, OPT OUT, CANCEL or UNSUBSCRIBE. Telemarketers must register with the Attorney General unless an exemption applies.
reply_or_inquiry_carveout: Not a telephone solicitation if sent with prior express written consent, about an existing debt or contract, or to someone with an established business relationship in the past 12 months. The old exclusion for calls made “in response to an express request” isn’t in the new definition.

covers_texts: Yes, for Chapter 302 (registration of telephone sellers): since September 1, 2025, a “telephone solicitation” includes a text or graphic message or image sent to induce a purchase (SB 140). Chapter 302 has its own exemptions.
quiet_hours: 9 a.m.–9 p.m.; Sun. noon–9 p.m. (calls)
quiet_hours_notes: 9 a.m.–9 p.m. Monday–Saturday and noon–9 p.m. Sunday (§301.051). SB 140 didn’t change Chapter 301, which speaks of a “consumer telephone call,” so whether these hours reach texts is unclear.
consent_limits_optout: SB 140 also made violations of Chapters 304 and 305 enforceable through the Deceptive Trade Practices Act, including private lawsuits.
reply_or_inquiry_carveout: §301.051 doesn’t apply to a call made in response to the consumer’s express request, or to a consumer with a prior or existing business relationship.

covers_texts: Yes. A “telephone solicitation” includes a text message to a Virginia area code or to a Virginia resident (§59.1-510, as amended in 2025).
quiet_hours_notes: 8 a.m.–9 p.m., unless the person gave you prior consent (§59.1-511).
consent_limits_optout: A text opt-out by replying “STOP” or “UNSUBSCRIBE” must be honored for at least 10 years (§59.1-514(A)).
reply_or_inquiry_carveout: For the opt-out and do-not-call section, a solicitation excludes contacts with an established business relationship, which includes the person’s inquiry about your goods or services in the previous 3 months (§59.1-510, §59.1-514(D)). That carve-out doesn’t apply to the hours rule.

covers_texts: Yes. No commercial text messages to a Washington resident’s phone (RCW 19.190.060) unless the recipient “clearly and affirmatively consented in advance” (RCW 19.190.070). “Commercial” means sent to promote goods or services for sale or lease (RCW 19.190.010).
quiet_hours: 8 a.m.–8 p.m. (calls)
quiet_hours_notes: 8 a.m.–8 p.m. for telephone solicitors (RCW 80.36.390(8)). That law defines a “telephone call” as one using a live person, artificial voice or recorded message, so it may not reach texts.
consent_limits_optout: Advance, affirmative consent for commercial texts. A 2025 state appeals decision read “commercial” broadly (recruiting texts counted), and review was sought in the state Supreme Court.
reply_or_inquiry_carveout: RCW 80.36.390 excludes calls made in response to a request or inquiry by the called party. The text-message law has no inquiry carve-out: what matters is whether the text promotes goods or services.
